6 The Bayesian Paradigm

Priors, Posteriors and Conjugacy

  1. 39.

    Suppose that the probability θ of producing a defective item in an automated manufacturing process is unknown.

    1. (a)

      A sample of n=8 items are to be selected at random. The total number of this sample found to be defective is represented as X. What is the distribution of X?

    2. (b)

      It is found that X=3 of the n=8 items are indeed defective. Write down the likelihood function ℓ⁢(θ).

    3. (c)

      Suppose the prior distribution of θ is a uniform distribution on the interval [0,1]. Determine the posterior distribution of θ, up to a multiplicative constant, using Bayes theorem for continuous variables.

    4. (d)

      Find the mode of the posterior distribution i.e. the value of θ that maximises the posterior distribution. This is often called the Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimate and denoted θ^M⁢A⁢P. Compare with the θ^M⁢L⁢E and comment.

    5. (e)

      Now suppose that the prior pdf for θ is instead f⁢(θ)=2⁢(1−θ) for 0≤θ≤1, and 0 otherwise. As before, suppose that three out of eight items are found to be defective. Determine the posterior distribution for θ, up to a multiplicative constant.

    6. (f)

      Find the MAP estimate θ^M⁢A⁢P in this case and compare with your answer to part (d).

    Solution

    1. (a)

      Each item has probability θ of being defective and as we are choosing them at random, this is a Binomial scenario. Therefore X∼B⁢i⁢n⁢(8,θ).

    2. (b)

      Binomial likelihood so

      ℓ⁢(θ)=f⁢(x|θ) = (nx)⁢θx⁢(1−θ)n−x
      = (83)⁢θ3⁢(1−θ)5
    3. (c)

      We have

      Prior: f⁢(θ) = 1,θ∈[0,1]
      Bayes theorem gives the Posterior: f⁢(θ|x) ∝f⁢(x|θ)⁢f⁢(θ)
      ∝(83)⁢θ3⁢(1−θ)5×1
      ⟹f⁢(θ|x) =k1⁢θ3⁢(1−θ)5

      where k1 is the unknown multiplicative constant (which is determined in Question 40.).

    4. (d)

      To find the mode we can either (i) notice that this posterior has the same shape as the likelihood in which case θ^M⁢A⁢P=θ^M⁢L⁢E=x/n=3/8, or, we can (ii) just use the same log trick as when we found the maximum likelihood estimate and find the maximum of the log posterior:

      log⁡(f⁢(θ|x)) =log⁡(k)+3⁢log⁡(θ)+5⁢log⁡(1−θ).
      ⟹∂∂θ⁢log⁡(f⁢(θ|x)) =3θ−51−θ=  0
      ⟹θ^M⁢A⁢P =38

      or we can (iii) use the attributes of Beta distributions (which we do in Question 40.). Method (ii) preferred here. To comment on this result, we would just note that as expected, θ^M⁢A⁢P is the same as the Maximum Likelihood Estimate θ^M⁢L⁢E as the prior is flat.

    5. (e)

      Similar to part (c) we have

      Prior: f⁢(θ) = 2⁢(1−θ),θ∈[0,1]
      Bayes theorem gives the Posterior: f⁢(θ|x) ∝f⁢(x|θ)⁢f⁢(θ)
      ∝(83)⁢θ3⁢(1−θ)5×2⁢(1−θ)
      ⟹f⁢(θ|x) =k2⁢θ3⁢(1−θ)6

      where k2 is the unknown multiplicative constant (again, which is determined in Question 40.).

    6. (f)

      Similar to part (d) however now θ^M⁢A⁢P≠θ^M⁢L⁢E, so we just use method (ii) which gives for the derivative of the log posterior:

      ∂∂θ⁢log⁡(f⁢(θ|x)) =3θ−61−θ=  0
      ⟹θ^M⁢A⁢P =39=13

      Comparing with the answer for part (d) we see that the MAP estimate is now slightly lower: the anticipated effect of a prior that mildly favoured lower values of θ.

  2. 40.

    [Exam standard] Consider the same scenario as in question 39., but now for the general case where n items are to be selected at random, and X=x are found to be defective.

    1. (a)

      Write down the likelihood function ℓ⁢(θ).

    2. (b)

      Suppose the prior distribution for θ was that of a Beta distribution with parameters a and b, that is θ∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(a,b). Show that this Beta distribution is conjugate for the likelihood you gave in part (a). [Reminder: a prior is conjugate if the posterior turns out to belong to the same family of distributions as the prior.]

    3. (c)

      Give the full posterior pdf for θ, including an expression for the multiplicative constant.

    4. (d)

      Which Beta distributions do the two priors used in question 39. correspond to?

    5. (e)

      Give the full posterior pdfs, including evaluating the multiplicative constants, corresponding to the two priors in Question 39.. Note, this will involve evaluating Gamma functions and remembering that Γ⁢(a)=(a−1)! for positive integer a.

    6. (f)

      For the general prior case θ∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(a,b) give the prior and posterior expectations of θ. Compare them and comment.

    7. (g)

      What is the behaviour of the posterior expectation as n→∞?

    Solution

    1. (a)

      Binomial scenario as before so the likelihood is:

      ℓ⁢(θ)=f⁢(x|θ)=(nx)⁢θx⁢(1−θ)n−x
    2. (b)

      If our prior is θ∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(a,b) then we have

      f⁢(θ)=1B⁢(a,b)⁢θa−1⁢(1−θ)b−1=Γ⁢(a+b)Γ⁢(a)⁢Γ⁢(b)⁢θa−1⁢(1−θ)b−1,0≤θ≤1 (13)

      Then the posterior becomes (using Bayes theorem):

      f⁢(θ|x) ∝f⁢(x|θ)⁢f⁢(θ)
      ∝(nx)⁢θx⁢(1−θ)n−x×1B⁢(a,b)⁢θa−1⁢(1−θ)b−1
      ∝θa+x−1⁢(1−θ)b+n−x−1

      We hence identify this with the core of a Beta distribution with parameters a+x and b+n−x, and hence the posterior is from the same family of distributions as the prior, and therefore this choice of Beta prior is indeed conjugate to the Binomial likelihood.

    3. (c)

      As we have shown that θ|x∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(a+x,b+n−x) we can identify the proportionality (or multiplicative) constant and write the full pdf:

      f⁢(θ|x)=1B⁢(a+x,b+n−x)⁢θa+x−1⁢(1−θ)b+n−x−1,0≤θ≤1
    4. (d)

      The first prior was θ∼U⁢n⁢i⁢f⁢(0,1) which has f⁢(θ)=1 for θ∈[0,1]. This corresponds to a B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(1,1) distribution. The second prior was f⁢(θ)= 2⁢(1−θ) which corresponds to a B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(1,2) distribution.

    5. (e)

      In Question 39. we had n=8 and x=3, so the first prior B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(1,1) gets updated to a posterior of B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(1+x,1+n−x)=B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(1+3,1+8−3)=B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(4,6). This has pdf

      f⁢(θ|x)=1B⁢(4,6)⁢θ3⁢(1−θ)5 =Γ⁢(10)Γ⁢(4)⁢Γ⁢(6)⁢θ3⁢(1−θ)5,0≤θ≤1
      =9!3!⁢ 5!⁢θ3⁢(1−θ)5
      = 504⁢θ3⁢(1−θ)5

      Similarly for the second prior B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(1,2) gets updated to a posterior of B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(1+x,2+n−x)=B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(1+3,2+8−3)=B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(4,7), which has pdf

      f⁢(θ|x)=1B⁢(4,7)⁢θ3⁢(1−θ)6 =Γ⁢(11)Γ⁢(4)⁢Γ⁢(7)⁢θ3⁢(1−θ)6,0≤θ≤1
      =10!3!⁢ 6!⁢θ3⁢(1−θ)6
      = 840⁢θ3⁢(1−θ)6
    6. (f)

      For general prior case θ∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(a,b) we have posterior θ∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(a+x,b+n−x) and

      Prior Expectation: E⁢[θ]= aa+b
      Posterior Expectation: E⁢[θ|x]= (a+x)(a+x)+(b+n−x)=a+xa+b+n

      We see that the posterior expectation is now an amalgamation of information from our prior expectation for θ and from the sample proportion =θ^M⁢L⁢E=x/n. In fact, as shown in lectures, the posterior expectation can be written as a weighted linear combination of these two objects: this is just the sort of behaviour we may want our statistical analysis to exhibit.

    7. (g)

      In the large n limit we can see (without resorting to too much rigour):

      E⁢[θ|x]=a+xa+b+n=xn+an1+a+bn→xn=θ^M⁢L⁢Eas⁢n→∞ (14)

      This is because a and b are fixed and hence a/n→0 and b/n→0, while the x/n term may not (in that it could be equal to zero if θ=0, but in all other cases it will tend to a finite amount >0). So the posterior expectation and the MLE agree in the large n limit, which is again comforting.

  3. 41.

    Suppose that the number of minutes X that a person must wait for a bus each morning has a uniform distribution on the interval [0,θ], where the value of the endpoint θ is unknown. So we have X|θ∼U⁢[0,θ].

    1. (a)

      Sketch a plot of the conditional pdf of X given θ, that is plot f⁢(x|θ) against x, clearly labelling θ.

    2. (b)

      If a single waiting time observation x1 is obtained, write down the likelihood ℓ⁢(θ) as a function of θ, remembering to specify clearly the values of θ for which the likelihood will be zero. [Hint: Uniform distributions over arbitrary ranges still have to integrate to 1.]

    3. (c)

      Sketch a plot of the likelihood ℓ⁢(θ) against θ, carefully labelling the location of x1.

    4. (d)

      Suppose that the prior pdf of θ is as follows:

      f⁢(θ)={192θ4for⁢θ≥4,0otherwise.

      If observed waiting times on three successive mornings are (5,3,8) minutes, what is the posterior pdf of θ?

    Solution

    1. (a)

      A plot of a uniform distribution between 0 and θ, with height 1/θ.

    2. (b)

      Following the hint, we remember that uniform distributions must integrate to 1, so have height equal to the reciprocal of their range, i.e.

      ℓ⁢(θ)=f⁢(x1|θ)={1/θfor⁢0<x1<θ,0otherwise.

      Note that when viewed as a function of θ, the condition x1<θ becomes very important, as does the 1/θ dependence.

    3. (c)

      A plot of ℓ⁢(θ) against θ which gives 0 for 0<θ<x1 and 1/θ for 0<x1<θ. Note that this is very different from the shape of the uniform distribution from part (a).

    4. (d)

      The joint pdf of the three observations (and also the likelihood) is

      ℓ⁢(θ)=f⁢(x1,x2,x3|θ)={1/θ3for⁢0<xi<θ(i=1,2,3),0otherwise.

      Therefore, the posterior pdf f⁢(θ|x1,x2,x3) will be non-zero only if θ≥4, as required by the prior pdf, and also θ>8, the largest of the three observed values. Hence, for θ>8,

      f⁢(θ|x1,x2,x3)∝f⁢(x1,x2,x3|θ)⁢f⁢(θ)∝1/θ7.

      Since

      ∫8∞1θ7⁢d⁢θ=[−θ−66]8∞=16⁢(8)6,

      it follows that

      f⁢(θ|x1,x2,x3)={6⁢(8)6θ7for⁢θ>8,0for⁢θ≤8.
  4. 42.

    [Exam standard] A Weibull distribution (with shape parameter fixed at the value 2), with scale parameter α>0, for a non-negative continuous random quantity X, has probability density function

    f⁢(x∣α)=2⁢α2⁢x⁢e−(α⁢x)2
    1. (a)

      Assume that n observations x1, … , xn are sampled from this distribution. Derive the likelihood function for α based on these data, and also derive the corresponding maximum likelihood estimate of α.

    2. (b)

      Show that conjugate priors for α can be specified by the probability density function

      f⁢(a)∝a2⁢ν⁢e−τ⁢a2

      for a>0 and with ν>0 and τ>0. Specify (up to proportionality constant) the corresponding posterior density function based on the observations x1,…,xn. Derive the modes of these prior and posterior distributions, and briefly discuss how the posterior mode relates to the mode of the prior distribution and the maximum likelihood estimate of α.

    3. (c)

      Explain carefully how one could interpret the parameters ν and τ of these prior distributions in part (b) in relation to sufficient statistics of the data.

    4. (d)

      Suppose that, in addition to the n observations x1, …, xn, for one further individual it was observed that the corresponding random value Xn+1>c, for some c>0, so not its actual value was observed but only that it exceeds c. Is it important to take this information into account? If so, briefly explain how one can take it into account when one uses the methods of parts (a) and (b). If you consider it not important that this information is taken into account, briefly explain why not.

    Solution

    1. (a)
      ℓ⁢(α∣x1,…,xn) =∏i=1n(2⁢α2⁢xi⁢e−(α⁢xi)2)=2n⁢α2⁢n⁢[∏i=1nxi]⁢e−α2⁢T
      ∝α2⁢n⁢e−α2⁢T,

      where T=∑ixi2 is a sufficient statistic, assuming we know n.

      ℒ=log⁡ℓ⁢(α∣x1,…,xn) =const+2⁢n⁢log⁡α−α2⁢T
      ∂ℒ∂α =2⁢nα−2⁢α⁢T
      =0⇔α^=(nT)12.

      ∂2L∂α2<0 so its a maximum.

    2. (b)

      Clearly, the given prior f⁢(α) has the same functional form as the likelihood above, and leads to a posterior of the form

      f⁢(α∣x1,…,xn)∝α2⁢(ν+n)⁢e−(τ+T)⁢α2,

      which is of the same form as the prior, hence the prior is indeed conjugate. Using the same argument as we used to find the MLE gives

      prior mode:α~0 =(ντ)12
      likelihood mode (MLE):α^ =(nT)12
      posterior mode:α~1 =(ν+nτ+T)12

      The prior mode is the square root of 1/(τ/ν), where τ/ν can be interpreted as the mean of hypothetical sample square values representing prior beliefs. The MLE is 1/x2¯, which is the mean of the observed sample squared values. The posterior mode is thus the square root of 1/w where w is a the weighted average between the sample data and prior beliefs.

    3. (c)

      If we suppose that our prior corresponded to some hypothetical sample y1, …, yν, then ν is the sample size and τ=∑i=1νyi2 for this hypothetical sample.

    4. (d)

      Yes, it is important. It would be taken into account via the likelihood function, and thus the posterior, by the inclusion of a term P⁢(Xn+1>c∣α) to the product. In the MLE, c2 will be added to T while n remains unchanged.

  5. 43.

    We saw the definition of the Beta distribution in lectures:

    Let X∼Beta⁢(a,b) for a,b>0 known. Then X has a Beta distribution with pdf

    f⁢(x)=1B⁢(a,b)⁢xa−1⁢(1−x)b−1=Γ⁢(a+b)Γ⁢(a)⁢Γ⁢(b)⁢xa−1⁢(1−x)b−1,0≤x≤1

    and 0 otherwise, where B⁢(a,b)=Γ⁢(a)⁢Γ⁢(b)Γ⁢(a+b) is the Beta function, Γ⁢(a) is the Gamma function and Γ⁢(a)=(a−1)! for a∈ℕ. The Gamma function also satisfies the more general statement Γ⁢(a+1)=a⁢Γ⁢(a) for a∈ℝ,a>0, which you will need.

    1. (a)

      Using the fact that, if X∼Beta⁢(a,b) then f⁢(x) must integrate to 1, show that the expectation of X is given by:

      E⁢[X]=aa+b
    2. (b)

      Similarly, find E⁢[X2].

    3. (c)

      Hence, show that:

      Var⁢[X]=a⁢b(a+b)2⁢(a+b+1)
    4. (d)

      Show that the mode, i.e. the value of x that maximises f⁢(x), is indeed given by:

      M⁢o⁢d⁢e⁢(X)=a−1a+b−2 for ⁢a,b>1

    Solution

    1. (a)

      The fact that, if X∼Beta⁢(a,b) then f⁢(x) must integrate to 1, implies that

      ∫01f⁢(x)⁢𝑑x = 1
      ⇔∫01Γ⁢(a+b)Γ⁢(a)⁢Γ⁢(b)⁢xa−1⁢(1−x)b−1⁢𝑑x = 1
      ⇔∫01xa−1⁢(1−x)b−1⁢𝑑x = Γ⁢(a)⁢Γ⁢(b)Γ⁢(a+b)

      so we can use this to solve any such integral, which is exactly what we need to find the expectation of X:

      E⁢[X] = ∫01x⁢f⁢(x)⁢𝑑x
      = ∫01x.Γ⁢(a+b)Γ⁢(a)⁢Γ⁢(b)⁢xa−1⁢(1−x)b−1⁢d⁢x
      = Γ⁢(a+b)Γ⁢(a)⁢Γ⁢(b)⁢∫01xa⁢(1−x)b−1⁢𝑑x
      = Γ⁢(a+b)Γ⁢(a)⁢Γ⁢(b)⁢Γ⁢(a+1)⁢Γ⁢(b)Γ⁢(a+1+b)

      we can now use the property of the Gamma function that Γ⁢(a+1)=a⁢Γ⁢(a) to simplify:

      E⁢[X] = Γ⁢(a+b)Γ⁢(a)⁢Γ⁢(a+1)Γ⁢(a+1+b)
      = Γ⁢(a+b)Γ⁢(a)⁢a⁢Γ⁢(a)(a+b)⁢Γ⁢(a+b)
      = aa+bas required.
    2. (b)

      Similarly,

      E⁢[X2] = ∫01x2⁢f⁢(x)⁢𝑑x
      = Γ⁢(a+b)Γ⁢(a)⁢Γ⁢(b)⁢∫01xa+1⁢(1−x)b−1⁢𝑑x
      = Γ⁢(a+b)Γ⁢(a)⁢Γ⁢(b)⁢Γ⁢(a+2)⁢Γ⁢(b)Γ⁢(a+2+b)
      = Γ⁢(a+b)Γ⁢(a)⁢Γ⁢(b)⁢(a+1)⁢Γ⁢(a+1)⁢Γ⁢(b)(a+b+1)⁢Γ⁢(a+b+1)
      = Γ⁢(a+b)Γ⁢(a)⁢Γ⁢(b)⁢(a+1)⁢a⁢Γ⁢(a)⁢Γ⁢(b)(a+b+1)⁢(a+b)⁢Γ⁢(a+b)
      = a⁢(a+1)(a+b+1)⁢(a+b)
    3. (c)

      We now have all we need to find the variance of X:

      Var⁢[X] = E⁢[X2]−E⁢[X]2
      = a⁢(a+1)(a+b+1)⁢(a+b)−(aa+b)2
      = a⁢(a+1)⁢(a+b)−a2⁢(a+b+1)(a+b+1)⁢(a+b)2
      = a⁢[a2+a⁢b+a+b−a2−a⁢b−a](a+b+1)⁢(a+b)2
      = a⁢b(a+b)2⁢(a+b+1)as required.
    4. (d)

      To find the mode we just differentiate the log of the pdf f⁢(x), and set it to zero:

      ∂∂x⁢log⁡[f⁢(x)] = ∂∂x⁢{log⁡[Γ⁢(a+b)Γ⁢(a)⁢Γ⁢(b)]+log⁡[xa−1]+log⁡[(1−x)b−1]}
      = 0+1xa−1⁢(a−1)⁢xa−2+1(1−x)b−1⁢(b−1)⁢(1−x)b−2.(−1)
      = (a−1)x−(b−1)(1−x)=  0
      ⇔ (1−x)⁢(a−1)=x⁢(b−1)
      ⇔ a−1−x⁢(a−1)=x⁢(b−1)
      ⇔ a−1=x⁢(a−1)+x⁢(b−1)
      ⇔ a−1=x⁢(a+b−2)
      ⇔ x=a−1a+b−2

      We note that in order for this mode to lie within the interval (0,1) (as it is an estimate for x) this implies both a>1 and b>1. We also examine the second derivative to check that it is a maximum:

      ∂2∂x2⁢log⁡[f⁢(x)] = ∂∂x⁢{(a−1)x−(b−1)(1−x)}
      = −(a−1)x2−(b−1)(1−x)2

      which is trivially negative if a>1 and b>1 and hence the mode is indeed a maximum. It is interesting to examine the following edge cases (even though the question does not ask for this) where either a=1 or b=1 (where it is possible for the mode to be on the boundary at x=0 or x=1). Here, it is best to just examine the Beta pdf directly. E.g. if (a=1 and b=1): uniform distribution with no unique mode; (b=1 and a>1): mode at x=1; (b=1 and a<1): mode at x=0 as pdf →∞ as x→0. Similarly, (a=1 and b>1): mode at x=0; (a=1 and b<1): mode at x=1 as pdf →∞ as x→1. Note also that if a,b<1 there is a minimum in the pdf (as the second derivative will be positive), and the are mode will be at one of the two boundaries x=0 or x=1.

Credible Intervals and the Normal-Normal Model

  1. 44.

    [Exam standard] Now we have learned a lot more about updating our beliefs about probabilities, we can advise the student in Question 1. She was told that she is about to play a game against an opponent who is a cheat, using a loaded dice which rolls a 6 more often than not. Let’s focus on just the events that a 6 is rolled or it is not, so we redefine: Xi=1: a 6 is rolled, and Xi=0: a 6 was not rolled, for the ith roll. The total number of times a 6 is rolled out of n rolls is denoted X=∑i=1nXi as usual and we see that X|p∼B⁢i⁢n⁢(n,p) where p=P⁢(Xi=1), the probability that a 6 is rolled on any individual roll.

    1. (a)

      The student had originally (in Question 1(b)) asserted that p=0.6 in response to the information that the dice “rolls a 6 more often than not”, but now realises that such a precise statement is somewhat dangerous. She instead wants to specify a Beta prior distribution for p that has

      E⁢[p]=0.6andVar⁢[p]=0.052

      implying that a prior interval of E⁢[p]±2⁢SD⁢[p]=[0.5,0.7]. Assuming p∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(a,b), find a and b to ensure this prior is consistent with her specified expectation and variance.

    2. (b)

      If she then plays the game and sees a total of x 6’s from a set of n rolls of the dice, write down the posterior distribution for p both for this general case, and for the case in Question 1(c) where n=1000 and x=550.

    3. (c)

      For the n=1000 and x=550 case give the posterior expectation E⁢[p|x], variance Var⁢[p|x] and standard deviation SD[p|x].

    4. (d)

      One has to wait a long time to see 1000 rolls of the dice. Write down her posterior after only n=50 rolls, when she has seen x=27 rolls that gave a 6. Calculate a 95% Credible Interval in this case using the normal approximation to the Beta distribution (which will be very accurate here).

    5. (e)

      Calculate the corresponding frequentist 95% Confidence Interval for the n=50 and x=27 case and compare to the Credible Interval found in part (d). What is the relative width of these intervals?

    6. (f)

      Examine the behaviour of the posterior variance Var⁢[p|x] for large n (i.e. when n and therefore x become large, but where n has not reached ∞), for constant a and b.

    7. (g)

      Hence, examine the behaviour of the 95% Credible Interval for large n (your answer to Q40(g) may help). Compare this behaviour to the 95% Confidence Interval and comment.

    Solution

    1. (a)

      We know from lectures (and proved in Q43) that the expectation and variance of p∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(a,b) are given by:

      E⁢[p]=aa+bandVar⁢[p]=a⁢b(a+b)2⁢(a+b+1)

      Setting these equal to 0.6 and 0.052 respectively gives:

      E⁢[p]=aa+b= 0.6⇔a= 0.6⁢a+0.6⁢b⇔0.4⁢a= 0.6⁢b⇔b=2⁢a3

      Inserting this into the variance constraint gives:

      Var⁢[p]=a⁢b(a+b)2⁢(a+b+1) = 0.052
      ⇔2⁢a2/3(a+2⁢a/3)2⁢(a+2⁢a/3+1) = 1202
      ⇔2⁢a2/3(5⁢a/3)2⁢(5⁢a/3+1) = 1202
      ⇔652⁢(5⁢a/3+1) = 1202
      ⇔1852⁢(5⁢a+3) = 1202
      ⇔18.20252 = (5⁢a+3)
      ⇔18.42 = 5⁢a+3
      ⇔288 = 5⁢a+3
      ⇔a = 57
      ⇒b = 2⁢a3=2.573= 38

      So a prior of p∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(a=57,b=38) gives E⁢[p]=0.6 and Var⁢[p]=0.052 as required.

    2. (b)

      We know that a Beta prior p∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(a,b) is conjugate to a Binomial likelihood X|p∼B⁢i⁢n⁢(n,p) and that the posterior will be simply p|X∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(a+x,b+n−x), so in the case where we have the particular prior p∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(a=57,b=38), the posterior is simply:

      p|x∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(57+x,38+n−x)

      In the specific case of Question 1(c) where n=1000 and x=550 we have simply:

      p|x∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(57+550,38+1000−550)
      ⇒ p|x∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(607,488)
    3. (c)

      Posterior expectation, variance and SD for a posterior p|x∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(a~,b~) are given by,

      E⁢[p|x] = a~a~+b~=(a+x)(a+x)+(b+n−x)=a+xa+b+n=6071095= 0.554
      Var⁢[p|x] = a~⁢b~(a~+b~)2⁢(a~+b~+1)=607.488(607+488)2⁢(607+488+1)
      = 607.48810952⁢.1096=  0.0002254082
      SD⁢[p|x] = Var⁢[p|x]=0.0002254082=  0.0150136.
    4. (d)

      After only n=50 rolls with x=27 the posterior will be p∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(a+x,b+n−x)=B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(57+27,38+50−27)=B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(84,61). Expectation, variance and SD will be:

      E⁢[p|x] = a~a~+b~=8484+61=  0.5793103
      Var⁢[p|x] = a~⁢b~(a~+b~)2⁢(a~+b~+1)=84.61(84+61)2⁢(84+61+1)=  0.001669246
      SD⁢[p|x] = Var⁢[p|x]=  0.0408564

      The approximate Normal 100⁢(1−α)% Credible Interval is given (with α=0.05) by:

      E⁢[p|x]±zα/2∗⁢Var⁢[p|x] = 0.5793103±1.96×0.0408564
      = [0.499,0.659](to 3 s.f.)

      Therefore, as this is a Credible Interval we can say (approximately) that:

      P⁢[0.499≤p≤0.659|x]≃  0.95
    5. (e)

      The frequentist 95% Confidence Interval is given by (with y=p^=x/n=27/50):

      95%⁢Confidence Interval = y±zα/2∗⁢y⁢(1−y)n
      = 2750± 1.96×2750⁢(1−2750)50
      = [0.401,0.678]

      The Confidence Interval is centered around a slightly lower value (27/50=0.54) than the Credible Interval (E⁢[p|x]=0.579) but most importantly the Confidence interval is wider than the Credible Interval, as the Confidence Interval has less information as it only uses the data and not the prior information. The width of the Confidence Interval is 0.276 (to 3 s.f.) and the Credible Interval is 0.160 (to 3 s.f) so we see the prior information has had a substantial impact, even after n=50 rolls. The relative size is 0.160/0.276=0.579 so the reduction is to about 58% of the Confidence Interval width.

    6. (f)

      The posterior variance is given, for general data and prior as

      Var⁢[p|x] = a~⁢b~(a~+b~)2⁢(a~+b~+1)
      = (a+x)⁢(b+n−x)((a+x)+(b+n−x))2⁢((a+x)+(b+n−x)+1)
      = (a+x)⁢(b+n−x)(a+b+n)2⁢(a+b+n+1)

      We now assume large n in that n≫1 and hence x≫1 (assuming p>0), but that the ratio y=x/n tends to a fixed value. Hence:

      Var⁢[p|x] = (a+x)⁢(b+n−x)(a+b+n)2⁢(a+b+n+1)
      = n2⁢(an+xn)⁢(bn+1−xn)n3⁢(1+a+bn)2⁢(1+a+b+1n)
      = (an+xn)⁢(bn+1−xn)n⁢(1+a+bn)2⁢(1+a+b+1n)
      ≃ (xn)⁢(1−xn)n
      = y⁢(1−y)n

      where we only kept the dominant terms in each bracket (and ignored terms that tend to zero for large n such as a/n, b/n etc.). This expression for Var⁢[p|x] for large n looks like the variance of the MLE estimate Var⁢[p^M⁢L⁢E]=y⁢(1−y)/n used in the Confidence Interval.

    7. (g)

      We already showed in Q40(g) that in the large n limit, E⁢[p|x]≃x/n=y. Therefore, for large n the Credible Interval is approximated by (using again the Normal approximation for Beta distributions, which will be very accurate in this case):

      E⁢[p|x]±zα/2∗⁢Var⁢[p|x] ≃ xn±zα/2∗⁢(xn)⁢(1−xn)n
      = y±zα/2∗⁢y⁢(1−y)n

      which agrees with the expression for the Confidence Interval used in part (e). We see therefore that in the limit of large amounts of data, the frequentist Confidence Interval and the Bayesian Credible interval converge to the same expressions: showing we can all agree when there is overwhelming amounts of data! Note that the interpretation of these two objects still remains different.

  2. 45.

    [Exam standard] Suppose that y1,…,yn is a random sample from a uniform distribution on (0,θ) where θ is an unknown positive parameter.

    1. (a)

      Show that the likelihood function ℓ⁢(θ) is given by ℓ⁢(θ)=1/θn for m<θ<∞ and 0 otherwise, where m=max⁡{y1,…,yn}.

    2. (b)

      Suppose that the prior distribution for θ is a Pareto distribution

      f⁢(θ)={a⁢baθa+1b<θ<∞0otherwise

      where a and b are specified positive constants. Show that the posterior distribution for θ is also Pareto with constants a+n and max⁡{b,m}.

    3. (c)

      Now put a=b=0 in the posterior distribution (corresponding to “vague” prior beliefs), and with this specification show that (m,m⁢α−1/n) is the 100⁢(1−α)% highest posterior density (HPD) credible interval for θ; that is, the posterior density at any point inside the interval is greater than that of any point outside the interval.

    Solution

    1. (a)

      The joint pdf is

      f⁢(y1,…,yn∣θ)={1/θnyi<θ<∞⁢ for ⁢i=1,…,n0otherwise

      But yi<θ<∞ for i=1,…,n is equivalent to m=max⁡{y1,…,yn}<θ<∞, since if m<θ then all yi<θ. When f⁢(y1,…,yn∣θ) is considered as a function of θ (for given data y1,…,yn) the likelihood is

      l⁢(θ)={1/θnm<θ<∞0otherwise
    2. (b)

      The prior for θ is

      f⁢(θ)={a⁢ba/θa+1b<θ<∞0otherwise

      The posterior for θ is

      f⁢(θ∣y1,…,yn)∝{1/θa+1+nb<θ<∞⁢ and ⁢m<θ<∞0otherwise

      But b<θ<∞⁢ and ⁢m<θ<∞ is equivalent to max⁡{b,m}<θ<∞. Hence, the posterior distribution for θ is Pareto with parameters a+n and max⁡{b,m}.

    3. (c)

      When a=b=0, the posterior is

      f⁢(θ∣y1,…,yn)={n⁢mn/θn+1m<θ<∞0otherwise

      Then

      ∫mm⁢α−1/nf⁢(θ∣y1,…,yn)⁢d⁢θ =∫mm⁢α−1/nn⁢mn/θn+1⁢d⁢θ
      =[−(mθ)n]mm⁢α−1/n=1−α

      Hence, the interval is a 100⁢(1−α)% credibility interval for θ. Inspection of the graph of the posterior f⁢(θ∣y1,…,yn) and noting that a) the posterior monotonically decreases with increasing θ (provided θ>m) and b) the posterior is zero for θ≤m, shows it to be a highest posterior density 100⁢(1−α)% credibility interval.

  3. 46.

    A random sample of n students is drawn from a large population, and their weights measured. The average weight of the n sampled students is x¯=150 pounds. Assume the weights in the population are normally distributed with unknown mean μ and known standard deviation 20 pounds. Suppose your prior distribution for μ is normal with mean 180 and standard deviation 40.

    1. (a)

      What is your posterior distribution for μ in terms of n?

    2. (b)

      Why would an Equal-tailed (EQT) posterior credible interval and a highest posterior density (HPD) credible interval give the same result for this posterior distribution?

    3. (c)

      For n=10 and n=100, find 95% posterior credible intervals for μ.

    Solution   

    1. (a)

      This is a conjugate normal sampling problem with known variance. Using notation from lectures, our prior for μ is μ∼N⁢(m=180,v2=t−1=402) and so the prior precision is t=1/402.

      Given μ, the data X1,…,Xn are i.i.d. with Xi∼N⁢(μ,σ2=τ−1=202) giving a data precision of τ=1/202.

      The posterior for μ∣x1,…,xn is N⁢(m1,v12=1/t1) where

      t1 =t+n⁢τ=1402+n202
      ⟹v12 =11402+n202
      m1 =t⁢m+n⁢τ⁢x¯t1=1402⁢180+n202⁢1501402+n202
    2. (b)

      The posterior is a normal distribution which is both symmetric and unimodal, hence a 100⁢(1−α)% EQT posterior credible interval will automatically have higher posterior density inside the interval than outside in the tails, and hence it will also be a 100⁢(1−α)% HPD interval.

    3. (c)

      Using n=10, we get m1=150.732 and v12=39.024=6.2472. Hence a 95% posterior credible interval for μ∣x1,…,xn is (either EQT or HPD give the same interval as argued in part (b)):

      m1±z∗⁢v1= 150.732±1.96×6.247=[138.488,162.976]

      For n=100, the posterior mean and variance become m1=150.075 and v12=1/t1=1/0.251=3.99=1.9982 respectively. Note that our posterior mean has not changed much, but the posterior variance has reduced substantially. The 95% posterior credible interval for μ∣x1,…,xn is

      m1±z∗⁢v1= 150.075±1.96×1.998=[146.160,153.990]
  4. 47.

    [Exam standard] An ornithologist is interested in the value of the mean height, μ, of the African fish eagle (Haliaeetus vocifer). The heights, X, of individual eagles have a normal distribution for which the value of the mean height μ is unknown but the standard deviation is known to be 2cm. Prior beliefs about μ can be adequately represented by a normal distribution with a mean of 68cm and a standard deviation of 1cm. A sample of 10 eagles are captured at random from the population, measured, and released, and their average height is found to be 69.5cm.

    1. (a)

      What is the posterior distribution of μ?

    2. (b)

      For both the prior and posterior distribution of μ, find the interval of length 1cm with the highest probability of containing μ. State the value of the probability associated with each interval. Comment on your results and justify any differences.

    3. (c)

      Consider the case where the number of eagles sampled, n, becomes very large. Show that the posterior for μ given the data will be Normal with mean, m1, and variance, v1 approximately given by m1≈x¯ and v12≈σ2n.

    Solution

    1. (a)

      The prior for μ is μ∼N⁢(68,12), so the prior precision is t=1.

      The individual heights are Xi  i.i.d N⁢(μ,22), so σ2=4 and τ=1/4. We have a sample of size n=10, and a sample mean x¯=69.5.

      This is a conjugate prior, so our posterior for μ∣x1,…,xn is given by the theorem from lectures:

      μ∣x1,…,xn∼N⁢(m1,v12=1t1)

      where t1=t+n⁢τ, and m1=t⁢m+n⁢τ⁢x¯t1.

      The values of the parameters are:

      t1 =1+10×14=3.5
      ⟹v12 =1t1=0.2857143
      m1 =1×68+10×69.5/43.5=69.07143

      Putting it all together, μ∣x1,…,xn∼N⁢(69.071,0.286).

    2. (b)

      The interval of highest probability corresponds to the highest (posterior) density interval (see the section on Credible Intervals in the notes). In this case, it is straightforward to see that this interval must be symmetric (because the distribution is), and centred about the mode. For the normal distribution, the mode is the same as the mean so we seek an interval of half-length 0.5 centred about the mean value. Trivially then, we obtain:

      Prior: 68±0.5=[67.5,68.5]
      Posterior: 69.071±0.5=[68.571,69.571]

      To find the probability of being in the interval, just manipulate the Normal probabilities, e.g. for the prior

      P⁢(67.5<μ<68.5) =P⁢(67.5−681<Z<68.5−681)
      =P⁢(|Z|<0.5)=2⁢Φ⁢(0.5)−1
      =0.3829249

      Similarly for the posterior

      P⁢(68.571<μ⁢<69.571∣⁢x1,…,xn) =P⁢(|Z|<0.5⁢3.5)
      =0.6504252

      We note that the posterior interval is associated with the higher probability. This is to be expected, as the posterior normal distribution has a smaller variance (v12=0.286) compared to the prior (v2=1) due to the update by the sample. Therefore, it concentrates more density (and hence probability) close to the mean, and so has higher probability for a central interval of fixed size.

    3. (c)

      Re-arrange the expressions for m1 and t1 and consider what happens if n grows very large:

      t1 =t+n⁢τ≈n⁢τ=nσ2⟹v12≈σ2n,
      m1 =t⁢m+n⁢τ⁢x¯t+n⁢τ=t⁢mn⁢τ+x¯tn⁢τ+1≈x¯
